title: Table VI: the production setting, and what the delta columns are actually measuring

what.formal: Table VI repeats the comparison under the production setting. Each dataset occupies three rows — Production, Transductive and Inductive — and four methods are reported (GBDT, HGNN, RD-HGNN, DD-HGNN) together with two difference columns, $\Delta_{GBDT}$ and $\Delta_{HGNN}$. The footer row is labelled "Avg. Rank/Avg." and carries average ranks for the four methods and average differences for the two delta columns.
what.plain: Same ten datasets, but now each is tested three ways: the combined production task, its transductive part, and its inductive part. Two extra columns report how much better the proposed models are than the two baselines.

what.md: **The three settings per dataset, and how they relate.** The production setting combines the two test sets, so its score is the headline. The transductive and inductive rows split that test set: transductive vertices were visible during training with their labels withheld, inductive ones were not present at all. A reader should therefore read the production row as a *blend* and the other two as its ingredients — and should not expect the production row to equal either one of them.

what.alt: Table VI of the paper: experimental results on ten datasets under the production setting
what.cap: Original Table VI (Feng et al., TPAMI 2026): three settings per dataset, four methods, and two difference columns.

example.md: **Walk 1 — the delta columns, and which model they use.** This is the part a reader cannot guess, so it has to be worked out. Take the Cora Production row: GBDT $74.30$, HGNN $81.91$, RD-HGNN $88.25$, DD-HGNN $86.48$, with printed deltas $\Delta_{GBDT} = +13.95$ and $\Delta_{HGNN} = +6.34$.

items.md: Test DD against the baselines: $86.48 - 74.30 = 12.18$ and $86.48 - 81.91 = 4.57$. Neither matches the printed deltas.
items.why: So the DD column is not the source, despite it being one of the paper's own models.
So the deltas are computed from RD-HGNN on this row — which is also the bolded entry, since RD edges out DD on Cora.

items.md: Now try a hypergraph dataset where DD wins. CA-Cora Production: GBDT $71.69$, HGNN $75.82$, RD $79.85$, DD $80.14$, printed $\Delta_{GBDT} = +8.45$.
items.why: DD − GBDT $= 8.45$ exactly, while RD − GBDT $= 8.16$. **Here the deltas are computed from DD.** So the column is not tied to one model.

items.md: Check the rule on all thirty rows: the deltas equal (the **better** of RD and DD) minus the baseline.
items.why: It holds on twenty-nine of the thirty rows, to within the rounding of the printed cells. **The delta columns therefore report the proposed method's best available number against each baseline, switching model from row to row without saying so** — which is a legitimate way to present results, but it means the deltas are not measuring one model's performance and cannot be averaged as if they were.

example.md: **Walk 2 — the one row that does not reconcile.** Github, Production: GBDT $85.69$, HGNN $86.05$, RD $85.93$, DD $85.96$. The printed $\Delta_{HGNN}$ is $+0.00$.

example.md: **This is the paper's cleanest numerical anomaly, and it is a sign error rather than a rounding error.** Both of the proposed models lose to the plain HGNN baseline on this row, by 0.12 and 0.09 points — small, but negative. Printing $+0.00$ removes the sign. The dedicated transductive and inductive rows for the same dataset behave differently ($+0.14$ and $-0.40$), so the anomaly is confined to this one cell. **Nothing about the paper's overall conclusion turns on it — but its position matters: it sits in the column that summarises how much better the proposed models are, and it converts a loss into a draw.**
**Walk 3 — the footer row.** The footer is labelled "Avg. Rank/Avg." and reads $4.0$, $2.8$, $1.7$, $1.5$ for the four methods and $+6.31$, $+2.53$ for the two delta columns.

example.md: **Note the label before the numbers: the same row mixes two different units.** Four entries are *average ranks* and two are *average point differences*, under a single heading. That is a presentational choice worth knowing about, because a reader skimming the bottom row will read six numbers as one family. And the two averages are not mutually consistent either: the $+2.53$ reproduces as the Production-row mean against HGNN using RD, while the $+6.31$ reproduces under no aggregation tried here — the same computation gives $5.94$.

quiz.q: Which model do Table VI's $\Delta$ columns compare against the baselines?

opts.md: DD-HGNN throughout, since it is the paper's full model
opts.expl: It is on some rows and not others. On Cora Production the deltas come from RD; on CA-Cora Production they come from DD. A single fixed model would give $12.18$ on Cora, not the printed $13.95$.

opts.md: Whichever of RD and DD scores higher on that row
opts.expl: Correct — verified on twenty-nine of the thirty rows. So the delta columns report the best of the two proposed models per row. That is defensible as a summary of "how much better is this paper", but it is not a fixed model's performance and cannot be averaged as one.

opts.md: The average of RD and DD
opts.expl: Averaging the two on Cora Production gives $13.07$, not the printed $13.95$; the columns track the maximum, not the mean.

quiz.q: For Github under the production setting, what is the correct $\Delta_{HGNN}$ from the printed cells? Give two decimals, with the sign.
quiz.hint: Use the better of the two proposed models on that row, and subtract the HGNN column.
quiz.sol: RD scores $85.93$ and DD $85.96$, so the better of the two is DD; $85.96 - 86.05 = -0.09$. The table prints $+0.00$. The magnitude is negligible but the sign is not: it is the difference between the proposed method edging past the baseline and failing to.

quiz.q: A results table has an extra column reporting the improvement of "our method" over a baseline. What is the first thing to establish?

opts.md: Whether the improvement is large enough to matter
opts.expl: Magnitude comes second. Until you know which quantity the column measures, the magnitude is not interpretable — a 6-point gap in one model's accuracy and a 6-point gap in the better of two models are different claims.

opts.md: Which model the column actually refers to, and whether it stays the same down the column
opts.expl: Correct. Here the reference model switches row by row, so the column is a per-row best rather than a measurement of one system. That is exactly the kind of thing a reader cannot infer from the header, and exactly what recomputing one cell reveals.

opts.md: Whether the baseline was tuned fairly
opts.expl: An important question, and a different one — it concerns the baseline column, not the derived column. Both matter, and neither substitutes for the other.
